body_markdown:
This calculator works out how much mulch you need from three inputs: the length and width of the bed, and the depth you want to spread. It reports the area, the volume in cubic feet, the volume in cubic yards, and the number of 2-cubic-foot bags. Change any box and the answer updates straight away.

## What the Result Means

The **square feet** figure confirms the area you measured. The **cubic feet** figure is the volume at your chosen depth. **Cubic yards** is what bulk suppliers quote, and the **bag count** is what you need if you are buying from a garden centre. All four describe the same quantity, so if the bag count looks high, check the depth setting rather than the area.

## Choosing the Right Depth

- **1 to 2 inches** refreshes beds that were mulched last year.
- **2 to 3 inches** is the standard for borders and flower beds.
- **3 to 4 inches** suits new beds going onto bare soil.
- **Over 4 inches** should be avoided against stems and trunks.

Depth is the input people get wrong most often, because a single inch of difference changes the volume by a third.

## A Worked Example

A bed 20 ft by 10 ft is 200 square feet. At 3 inches deep, that is 200 x 0.25 = 50 cubic feet, which is 1.85 cubic yards, or 25 bags of 2 cubic feet. Change the depth to 2 inches and the volume drops to 33 cubic feet, about 17 bags. That is why the calculator asks for depth first.

## Comparing Common Bed Sizes

- **100 sq ft at 3 in:** 25 cubic feet, 0.93 cubic yards, 13 bags.
- **200 sq ft at 3 in:** 50 cubic feet, 1.85 cubic yards, 25 bags.
- **400 sq ft at 3 in:** 100 cubic feet, 3.70 cubic yards, 50 bags.
- **500 sq ft at 3 in:** 125 cubic feet, 4.63 cubic yards, 63 bags.

The bag count assumes 2-cubic-foot bags, which is the most common size. If your supplier sells 1.5-cubic-foot bags, divide the cubic feet by 1.5 instead.

## Quick Conversions

There are 27 cubic feet in a cubic yard, so divide cubic feet by 27 for yards. A cubic yard is 13.5 bags of 2 cubic feet. If you are quoted a price per yard and a price per bag, divide the yard price by 13.5 to compare honestly.

## Measuring a Bed That Is Not a Rectangle

Split an L-shaped bed into two rectangles, work out each, and add them. For a curved bed, measure the widest and narrowest points and use the average. Write the measurements down in feet before using the calculator, so you are not converting in your head.

## Common Mistakes

- Using last year's depth without checking the bed today.
- Measuring the planting area but mulching the whole bed, or the reverse.
- Forgetting that mulch settles, so one thick layer looks thin a month later.
- Buying to the exact figure with no small margin for odd corners.

## How to Use the Result

Round up to the next whole bag, or add about 5 per cent when ordering bulk. Keep mulch a few inches clear of stems and trunks, and water the bed before you spread rather than after. If you are close to a whole cubic yard, order the whole yard; a second trip usually costs more than the extra material.

## Applying Mulch Without Mistakes

Spread in small piles across the bed rather than one heap, then level each pile with a rake or fork. This keeps the depth even, which matters more than it sounds: a bed that is three inches at the front and one inch at the back will grow weeds exactly where you cannot see them.

Keep the mulch a few inches away from the base of every stem, trunk and shrub. Piling it against bark traps moisture and is one of the most common causes of rot in young trees and shrubs. Feather the outer edge down to nothing so the bed blends into the lawn rather than ending in a ridge that sheds water onto the path.

Water the ground before you mulch, not after. Dry soil under a thick layer stays dry, because the mulch sheds the rain you are counting on. If you are mulching in summer, water thoroughly the day before, then spread the next morning while the soil is still damp.

Reapply thinly each year rather than deeply once. A fresh inch on top of last year's layer is usually enough to keep beds looking well and to stay ahead of weeds, and it avoids the slow build-up that smothers plant crowns.

faq.q: How deep should mulch be?
faq.a: Two to three inches for most beds. More than four inches can hold too much moisture against stems.

faq.q: How many bags of mulch is a cubic yard?
faq.a: Thirteen and a half 2-cubic-foot bags, since a cubic yard is 27 cubic feet.

faq.q: When is the best time to mulch?
faq.a: Early spring, after the soil has warmed, and again in autumn if you want winter protection.

faq.q: Does mulch prevent weeds?
faq.a: It suppresses most weeds if the layer is at least two inches deep and kept clear of plant stems.

body_markdown:
This calculator works out how much soil a raised bed needs from three inputs: the bed length, its width, and the fill depth. It returns the volume in cubic feet, cubic yards and bags, so you can order bulk or buy bagged mix without doing the arithmetic yourself.

## What the Result Means

The **cubic feet** figure is the raw volume. **Cubic yards** is what bulk topsoil suppliers sell. The **bag count** assumes 2-cubic-foot bags, so divide the cubic feet by your bag size if yours differ. A cubic yard is 27 cubic feet, or about 13.5 bags.

## Deciding the Fill Depth

- **Six inches** suits herbs, lettuce and shallow-rooted salad crops.
- **Ten to twelve inches** covers most vegetables and flowers.
- **Twelve to eighteen inches** suits carrots, parsnips and tomatoes.

If the bed sits on open ground, roots can grow below the frame, so you can fill it more shallowly. If it sits on concrete or gravel, the bed is the whole root zone and should be filled to full depth.

## A Worked Example

A bed 8 ft by 4 ft is 32 square feet. Filled 12 inches deep, that is 32 x 1 = 32 cubic feet, or 1.19 cubic yards, or 16 bags of 2 cubic feet. At 6 inches the volume halves to 16 cubic feet, and at 18 inches it rises to 48 cubic feet.

## Common Bed Sizes

- **4 x 4 ft at 6 in:** 8 cubic feet, 8 bags.
- **4 x 8 ft at 6 in:** 16 cubic feet, 8 bags.
- **4 x 8 ft at 12 in:** 32 cubic feet, 16 bags.
- **4 x 8 ft at 18 in:** 48 cubic feet, 24 bags.

## Mixing Your Own Blend

A dependable raised-bed mix is about 60 per cent topsoil, 30 per cent compost and 10 per cent perlite or coarse sand. This drains well and holds nutrients without compacting. Fresh manure should be composted first; used raw it burns young roots.

## Filling the Bed Well

Fill in layers and water each one so the mix settles before the next goes on. Stop about two inches below the rim. That freeboard stops soil washing out in rain and gives you room to top up. Expect the mix to settle by about a tenth of its volume in the first season.

## Common Mistakes

- Filling with garden soil straight from the ground, which compacts and drains poorly.
- Skipping drainage when the bed stands on a hard surface.
- Filling to the brim, so the first storm spills soil over the sides.
- Forgetting that the bed will need a top-up the following spring.

## How to Use the Result

If you are under about a cubic yard, bagged mix is easier and lets you choose the blend. Past that, order bulk, but check the delivery charge and make sure you can wheel it to the bed. Mix and fill in layers, and keep a bag in reserve for the spring top-up.

## Preparing the Site Before You Fill

Decide where the bed will sit before you order soil, because a full raised bed is far too heavy to move. Level the ground underneath, and remove turf or weeds so they do not grow up through the mix. If the bed stands on concrete or gravel, lay a sheet of landscape fabric first to slow drainage loss and stop weeds from the edges.

Think about access as well as sunlight. Leave enough room to walk and kneel all the way round the bed; a bed against a wall is only fully workable from three sides. Most vegetables want six to eight hours of sun, so watch the site through a day before you commit.

If the ground below is compacted or heavy clay, fork it over before the bed goes down. Roots will grow into it if it is loose, which effectively adds depth to the bed for free. On concrete or paving, there is no below, so fill to the full depth the crop needs.

Finally, line the base of a wooden bed with a single layer of cardboard. It suppresses weeds for the first season and then rots down, adding a little organic matter without blocking drainage.

body_markdown:
This calculator works out how much gravel a path, drive or border needs from the length, width and depth of the area. It reports square feet, cubic yards and tons, using a standard 1.4 tons per cubic yard for 3/4-inch crushed stone. Change any input and the result updates immediately.

## What the Result Means

**Square feet** is your measured area. **Cubic yards** is what most suppliers quote. **Tons** is what you need if the yard sells aggregate by weight. The tonnage assumes 3/4-inch crushed stone; finer or heavier stone changes the figure, so confirm it with your supplier before ordering by weight.

## Choosing the Right Depth

- **2 inches** for a decorative border or a light footpath.
- **3 inches** for a garden path over landscape fabric.
- **4 inches** for a light driveway, compacted in two layers.
- **6 inches** for regular vehicle traffic and parking.

Depth is the input with the biggest effect on cost. Doubling the depth doubles the material, so measure the job before choosing.

## A Worked Example

A path 20 ft by 10 ft is 200 square feet. At 3 inches deep, that is 200 x 0.25 = 50 cubic feet, or 1.85 cubic yards, which is about 2.6 tons. Spread to 4 inches for a drive and it becomes 66.7 cubic feet, 2.47 cubic yards, about 3.5 tons.

## Common Job Sizes

- **100 sq ft at 3 in:** 25 cubic feet, 0.93 cubic yards, 1.3 tons.
- **200 sq ft at 3 in:** 50 cubic feet, 1.85 cubic yards, 2.6 tons.
- **200 sq ft at 4 in:** 66.7 cubic feet, 2.47 cubic yards, 3.5 tons.
- **360 sq ft at 4 in:** 120 cubic feet, 4.44 cubic yards, 6.2 tons.

## Stone Choice Matters

Angular crushed stone locks together under a compactor and keeps its shape, which is what a driveway needs. Rounded pea gravel rolls and ruts, and belongs on borders and paths. For a drive, lay the sub-base, compact it, then add the stone in two layers rather than one.

## Conversions

There are 27 cubic feet in a cubic yard. A cubic yard of 3/4-inch crushed stone weighs about 1.4 tons. If the supplier quotes per ton, multiply your cubic yards by 1.4; if per yard, divide the ton price by 1.4 to compare.

## Common Mistakes

- Laying gravel onto bare soil without fabric, so it sinks and weeds grow through.
- Skipping compaction, leaving a loose surface that ruts.
- Using rounded stone where angular stone is needed.
- Ordering the exact volume with no margin for settlement.

## How to Use the Result

Add about 10 per cent for settlement and spreading losses, and have the load tipped as close to the work as the truck can reach. Keep a steel or timber edge at the boundary so the stone does not spread into the garden underfoot or under wheels.

## Laying Gravel Properly

Order the stone in two grades if you are building a drive: a coarser sub-base and a finer top layer. Spread the sub-base first, rake it level, then compact it before the top layer goes on. Compacting each layer separately is what stops the surface rutting under a wheel later.

Work from the far end of the job back toward the entrance, so you are not walking over finished stone. Use the back of a rake to level, then a plate compactor or a heavy roller to settle it. Aim for a slight crown in the middle of a path so water runs off to the sides rather than sitting in the middle.

Set the edging before the final layer, not after. A steel or timber edge holds everything in place, and retrofitting one means pulling stone back out. Leave the edging a few millimetres above the finished surface so the stone does not spill over it underfoot.

Once laid, top up any thin patches and re-compact. Gravel settles over the first few weeks, so keep a bag or two aside to dress the surface again after a month of use.

faq.a: Roughly 1.4 tons for 3/4-inch crushed stone, though it varies by stone type.

faq.q: How deep should gravel be for a driveway?
faq.a: Four inches compacted for a light drive, six inches for regular vehicle traffic.

faq.q: Can I put gravel directly on soil?
faq.a: Yes for paths, but lay landscape fabric first to stop the gravel sinking into the soil.

faq.q: How many tons of gravel in a cubic yard?
faq.a: About 1.3 to 1.5 tons depending on the stone, with 1.4 tons a good default.

body_markdown:
This calculator works out how much paint a room needs from its length, width and wall height, the number of coats, and the doors and windows to subtract. It returns the paintable area and the volume of paint in gallons, so you buy the right amount in one trip.

## What the Result Means

The **wall area** is the perimeter multiplied by the height, less the openings. The **gallons** figure assumes about 350 square feet of coverage per gallon, which is typical for a smooth, primed wall. Rougher or unprimed surfaces cover less, so add a little if that is your situation.

## Inputs Explained

- **Length and width** set the room's footprint and therefore the perimeter.
- **Wall height** is usually 8 ft, but measure the tallest wall if the ceiling slopes.
- **Coats** is two for almost every job, and a colour change may need a primer plus two.
- **Doors and windows** are subtracted at about 21 and 15 square feet each.

## A Worked Example

A room 12 ft by 10 ft with 8 ft walls has a perimeter of 44 ft and a wall area of 352 square feet. Subtract one door and two windows, about 51 square feet, leaving 301 square feet. Two coats is 602 square feet, and dividing by 350 gives about 1.7 gallons, so buy two.

## Common Room Sizes

- **10 x 10 ft, 2 coats:** about 1.5 gallons, buy 2.
- **12 x 10 ft, 2 coats:** about 1.7 gallons, buy 2.
- **12 x 12 ft, 2 coats:** about 1.9 gallons, buy 2.
- **14 x 12 ft, 2 coats:** about 2.2 gallons, buy 3.

## Ceilings and Trim

If you are painting the ceiling, add its length x width to the total. Trim, skirting and frames are measured in linear feet and painted separately, usually about a gallon per 100 to 150 feet. Together these often add a third to the job, so price them in from the start.

## Buying and Storing

Buy all the paint at once so it comes from a single batch; paint does not match across batches. Keep a labelled tin of each colour for touch-ups. If you are changing colour, expect a primer and possibly a third coat, particularly for strong colours on pale walls.

## Common Mistakes

- Buying for one coat and running short on the second.
- Not subtracting doors and windows, which over-buys by up to a gallon.
- Assuming a glossy surface needs no preparation; it usually needs keying or a bonding primer.
- Forgetting that a high or sloping ceiling adds a surprising amount of area.

## How to Use the Result

Round up to the next whole gallon or tin, and keep the spare. Two coats give an even finish; one coat rarely does, however good the paint. Cut in the edges first and keep a wet edge so you are not painting over a drying line.

## Estimating for More Than One Room

If you are painting several rooms, work out each one separately, then add the totals before you convert to gallons. Rooms differ in ceiling height, window count and number of coats, so a single averaged figure quickly drifts from reality. A small spreadsheet or a note per room keeps it straight.

Consider buying in larger tins. They usually cost less per litre than small ones, they guarantee the whole job comes from one batch, and you are less likely to run out halfway through a wall. Keep the leftover in a labelled tin for touch-ups, with the colour code written on the lid.

Do not forget the parts that the four walls miss: the ceiling, the skirting, the door and window frames, and any fitted furniture you plan to repaint. These are often measured in linear feet rather than square feet, and together they can add a third again to the paint you need.

Finally, buy the primer at the same time as the topcoat if you are changing colour or painting new plaster. A second trip for primer after the walls are cleared is the most common delay on a decorating job.

faq.a: Two coats for a colour change, and often two even when refreshing the same colour.

faq.a: Keep about 10% spare for touch-ups, and note the colour code for future matching.

body_markdown:
This calculator works out how many tiles a floor needs from the room length and width, the tile width and height, and the waste allowance. It returns the floor area, the number of tiles, and the count including waste, so you order enough in one go.

## What the Result Means

The **floor area** is length times width. The **tiles** figure is the floor area divided by the area of one tile. The **including waste** figure adds your chosen percentage for cuts and breakage, which is the number to order.

## Setting the Waste Allowance

- **10 per cent** for a straight grid, which covers edge cuts and the odd breakage.
- **15 per cent** for a diagonal or diamond layout, where every edge is a triangle cut.
- **More** for herringbone and other patterned layouts.

Waste is not optional. Every layout has edges, and edges mean cuts.

## A Worked Example

A room 12 ft by 10 ft is 120 square feet. With 12 x 12 inch tiles, each covering 1 square foot, that is 120 tiles. Adding 10 per cent gives 132, so order 132 tiles, or enough boxes to cover 132 square feet. Larger tiles cover more each, so the count falls even though the floor does not.

## Tile Count by Size

- **12 x 12 in (1 sq ft):** 120 tiles, 132 with waste.
- **12 x 24 in (2 sq ft):** 60 tiles, 66 with waste.
- **6 x 6 in (0.25 sq ft):** 480 tiles, 528 with waste.
- **8 x 8 in (0.44 sq ft):** about 273 tiles, 300 with waste.

## Buy by Box Coverage

Tile is sold by the box, and the box states its coverage in square feet. Read that figure rather than the tile count. If a box covers 10 square feet, a 120 square foot floor with waste needs about 14 boxes, whatever the individual tile size happens to be.

## Layout and Grout

Plan from the centre of the room so the cut tiles at opposite walls match. Dry-lay a row at doorways so two rooms meet on a full tile where possible. Grout joints add a couple of millimetres per tile, which can nudge the count on a large floor; the waste allowance usually covers it.

## Common Mistakes

- Ordering the exact area and ignoring cuts.
- Mixing dye lots from separate orders, which shows as a patchwork.
- Counting tiles instead of checking box coverage.
- Returning every spare box and having nothing left for a repair.

## How to Use the Result

Round up to whole boxes, and keep one box aside for future repairs. Buy everything at once so it comes from a single dye lot. Check the box coverage against your square footage before you order, and confirm the return policy in case you over-buy.

## Tools and Preparation for Laying Tile

Have the right tools before you start: a notched trowel, a tile cutter or wet saw, spacers, a spirit level, a rubber mallet, and a mixing bucket for adhesive. For large-format tiles you will also want a levelling clip system, which stops the corners from lipping where two tiles meet.

Preparation decides the finish. The floor must be clean, dry, flat and sound. Check the flatness with a straight edge; most adhesive instructions state a maximum variation, often a few millimetres over a metre. If the floor is uneven, use a levelling compound first, because no amount of care in laying will hide a bump.

Plan the whole layout before the first tile goes down. Mark the centre lines, dry-lay a row in both directions, and check the edge cuts. Starting from the wrong point leaves a sliver of tile at one wall, which no grout can disguise.

Work in small areas so the adhesive does not skin over before you place the tile. Press each tile down and twist slightly to spread the adhesive, and check with a level as you go rather than at the end.

faq.a: Add 10% for straight layouts and 15% for diagonal or patterned work.

faq.a: It varies by size; check the box coverage in square feet rather than counting tiles.

faq.q: Do I need to account for grout lines?
faq.a: Yes for precise work, though the waste allowance usually covers the small difference.

faq.q: Can I return leftover tile?
faq.a: Often yes if unopened and from the same batch, but dye lots differ, so buy all you need at once.

This calculator works out how much grass seed a lawn needs from its area and whether you are sowing a new lawn or overseeding an existing one. It returns the seed weight in pounds and the number of 3 lb bags, so you buy the right amount.

## What the Result Means

The **pounds** figure is the total seed weight for the method you choose. The **bags** figure converts that to 3 lb bags. A new lawn needs roughly 4 to 5 pounds per 1,000 square feet; overseeding needs about half that, because existing grass already covers much of the ground.

## New Lawn or Overseed

- **New lawn:** bare ground, sown at the full rate, roughly 4 to 5 lb per 1,000 sq ft.
- **Overseed:** thinning lawn, sown at about 2 lb per 1,000 sq ft to fill the gaps.

Using the new-lawn rate when overseeding wastes seed and can smother the grass you are trying to thicken.

## A Worked Example

A lawn of 5,000 square feet being overseeded needs about 10 pounds of seed, or four 3 lb bags. If the same lawn were bare ground being sown fresh, it would need 20 to 25 pounds. That difference is the whole reason the calculator asks for the method.

## Common Lawn Sizes

- **500 sq ft overseed:** about 1 lb.
- **1,000 sq ft overseed:** about 2 lb.
- **2,500 sq ft overseed:** about 5 lb.
- **5,000 sq ft overseed:** about 10 lb.

## Preparation Decides the Result

Seed fails more from poor preparation than from the rate. Mow short, rake out thatch, and aerate compacted ground. Seed needs contact with soil; on top of thatch it dries out and never sprouts. After sowing, rake lightly so the seed is barely covered, and firm the surface.

## Timing and Watering

Early autumn is the easiest window: warm soil, reliable rain, slowing weeds. Spring works but the young grass then faces summer heat. Keep the top inch damp for two weeks with light, frequent watering, then water more deeply and less often once the grass is up. Stay off the new lawn until it is rooted.

## Common Mistakes

- Sowing at the new-lawn rate when overseeding.
- Sowing onto hard or thatchy ground without preparation.
- Letting the seed dry out in the first fortnight.
- Burying the seed too deep to reach the light.

## How to Use the Result

Round up to the next bag and keep a little spare for the thin patches you will notice a month later. Divide your area by 1,000, multiply by the rate for your method, and order in one go so the seed is fresh.

## Choosing a Seed Mix

Seed is sold as mixes, and the right mix depends on the lawn and the light. A hard-wearing mix for a family lawn usually leans on ryegrass, which establishes quickly and takes traffic. A shade mix uses fescues that tolerate lower light under trees or beside walls. A fine mix for a decorative lawn uses bentgrass and fescue for a tighter sward.

Match the mix to the job. Overseeding an existing lawn works best with a mix similar to what is already growing, so the new and old grasses knit together at the same height and colour. Starting a new lawn gives you a free choice, so pick for the light and the use rather than for price alone.

Check the sow-by date on the bag. Seed loses viability over time, and old seed germinates unevenly, which shows as a patchy lawn. Buy fresh, and store any spare in a cool, dry place rather than a damp shed.

Finally, keep a note of the mix you used. When you top up thin patches later, matching the mix keeps the lawn one colour rather than a patchwork of different grasses.

This calculator works out how much concrete a slab needs from its length, width and thickness. It returns the volume in cubic yards and the number of 60 lb or 80 lb bags, so you can choose between mixing by hand and ordering ready-mix.

## What the Result Means

**Cubic yards** is the unit ready-mix suppliers use. The **bag count** assumes a fixed yield per bag, about 0.6 cubic feet for an 80 lb bag and 0.45 for a 60 lb bag. Both describe the same volume, so compare the bag cost against ready-mix per yard before deciding.

## Choosing the Thickness

- **4 inches** for paths, patios and light garden slabs.
- **5 inches** for a drive taking occasional cars.
- **6 inches** for regular vehicle traffic and heavy loads.

Thickness is set by what the slab carries, not by the budget. A slab too thin for its load cracks in the first winter.

## A Worked Example

A slab 10 ft by 10 ft at 4 inches is 100 square feet x 0.333 ft, which is 33.3 cubic feet, or 1.23 cubic yards. In 80 lb bags that is about 56; in 60 lb bags, about 74. At 6 inches the volume rises to 50 cubic feet, or 84 bags of 80 lb.

## Common Slab Sizes

- **6 x 6 ft at 4 in:** 12 cubic feet, 20 bags of 80 lb.
- **8 x 8 ft at 4 in:** 21.3 cubic feet, 36 bags.
- **10 x 10 ft at 4 in:** 33.3 cubic feet, 56 bags.
- **10 x 10 ft at 6 in:** 50 cubic feet, 84 bags.

## Ready-Mix or Bags

Past about one cubic yard, ready-mix is faster and usually cheaper, though most suppliers have a minimum load and the pour cannot wait. Bagged mix suits fence footings, steps, small pads and repairs. A 10 x 10 slab is near the limit of what is practical to mix by hand.

## Mixing and Curing

Mix only what you can place within about half an hour, and mix it stiff rather than wet; extra water weakens the set concrete. Use the water stated on the bag. After the pour, cover the slab and let it cure slowly for several days, and cut control joints so any cracking follows a straight line.

## Common Mistakes

- Making the slab too thin for the load it carries.
- Pouring onto soft or uneven ground without a compacted base.
- Adding too much water to make the mix easier to move.
- Letting the slab dry in the sun instead of curing slowly under cover.

## How to Use the Result

Add 5 to 10 per cent for spillage and uneven ground, and compare the bag total against a ready-mix quote including its minimum charge. Have formwork, reinforcement mesh and helpers ready before either route, because once a pour starts it cannot pause.

## Tools and Safety for a Small Pour

A small pour needs less equipment than people expect, but it needs the right pieces. Have a wheelbarrow or mixing tub, a hoe or paddle mixer, a shovel, a float and a trowel, a straight edge or screed board, and formwork boards with pegs. For anything beyond a small pad, hire a mixer, because mixing bag after bag by hand wears out a small team quickly.

Concrete is alkaline and dries the skin, so wear gloves and eye protection, and avoid kneeling in wet mix. Mix in a well-ventilated spot, and never add more water than the bag states to make it easier to move; the strength comes from a stiff mix, and extra water is the most common reason a slab fails.

Set the formwork square before you mix anything. Check the diagonals are equal, which is the simplest way to confirm a true rectangle, and peg the boards so they cannot bow under the weight of the mix. Lay any reinforcement mesh on small spacers so it sits in the lower third of the slab rather than on the ground.

Once the pour is finished, clean your tools immediately. Set concrete is far harder to remove than wet, and a barrow left overnight is a job nobody wants the next morning.

The short answer: **500 square feet at the standard 3-inch depth needs 125 cubic feet, which is 4.63 cubic yards, or 63 bags of 2-cubic-foot mulch.** If you plan to spread it thinner or thicker, the amount moves quickly, so it is worth checking the depth before you order.

## Working It Out for 500 Square Feet

The maths is short. Multiply the area by the depth in feet, then convert.

- **At 2 inches:** 500 x 0.167 = 83 cubic feet, or 3.1 cubic yards, about 42 bags.
- **At 3 inches:** 500 x 0.25 = 125 cubic feet, or 4.6 cubic yards, about 63 bags.
- **At 4 inches:** 500 x 0.333 = 167 cubic feet, or 6.2 cubic yards, about 84 bags.

That spread is the reason two gardeners with the same 500 square feet can buy wildly different amounts. The area is fixed; the depth is the choice.

## What 500 Square Feet Looks Like

It helps to picture the bed before you measure. Five hundred square feet is roughly a 20 x 25 ft bed, or ten beds of 50 square feet each. If your space is irregular, break it into rectangles, work out each one, and add them. A curved bed can be treated as a rectangle that just contains it, which adds a small safety margin.

## Bags or Bulk for This Size

At 4.6 cubic yards you are past the point where bags make sense. Bagged mulch is convenient for a couple of beds, but 63 bags is heavy, slow and usually more expensive per cubic foot than bulk. Call a supplier and ask for about 5 cubic yards of shredded hardwood or pine bark. They will tip it in one place, which is the one drawback: you then move it wheelbarrow by wheelbarrow.

If bulk delivery is not practical, bags still work. Buy a few extra and keep them dry; unopened bags store fine and save a second trip mid-job.

## Choosing the Depth

Depth depends on what the bed needs, not on what looks tidy.

- A refresh over last year's mulch is fine at 2 inches.
- Most flower beds and borders want 2 to 3 inches.
- New beds going onto bare soil want 3 to 4 inches to suppress weeds.
- Never go past 4 inches against trunks and stems, because trapped moisture causes rot.

## Prepare Before You Spread

Weed the bed first. Mulch suppresses weeds, but it does not kill the ones already growing, and they will push through. Water the ground well, then spread. Keep the mulch a few inches clear of stems and trunks, and feather it out to nothing at the edge of the bed rather than ending in a ridge.

## Ordering Checklist

- Re-measure the bed; 500 square feet is easy to overshoot with a rough guess.
- Confirm the depth for this bed rather than the one you mulched last year.
- Add about 5 per cent for settlement and odd corners.
- Ask whether the supplier sells by the cubic yard or by the scoop, and whether delivery is included.

## Frequently Confused Point

A cubic yard is not a bag. A cubic yard is 27 cubic feet, which is 13.5 bags of the 2-cubic-foot size. If someone quotes you a price per yard and you are comparing it with a price per bag, divide the yard price by 13.5 to compare fairly. That one step stops most people overpaying for bags on a job this size.

## Mulching Around Trees and Shrubs

Trees and shrubs need a different approach from a flower bed. Spread the mulch in a wide, flat ring out to the drip line, where the roots actually are, rather than a narrow mound at the trunk. Keep it several inches clear of the bark, so the trunk can stay dry.

The old habit of piling mulch into a cone against the trunk, sometimes called a mulch volcano, does real damage. It holds moisture against the bark, encourages rot and pests, and can cause roots to grow upward into the mulch instead of outward into the soil. A flat ring a few inches thick is both healthier and just as tidy.

For a 500 square foot area planted with shrubs, treat each one as a circle and add the rings together, or simply mulch the whole bed at a flat two to three inches and keep the mulch off the stems as you go. The total volume is the same idea: area times depth, with the stems left clear.

Refresh the ring each spring rather than rebuilding it, and pull any mulch that has drifted against a trunk back out with a rake.

**A raised bed needs length x width x depth in feet, converted to cubic yards for bulk or divided by the bag size for bags.** An 8 x 4 ft bed filled 12 inches deep takes 32 cubic feet, which is about 1.2 cubic yards or 16 bags of 2-cubic-foot soil.

## Soil by Bed Size

The volume changes fast with depth, so match the depth to what you are growing.

- **4 x 4 ft, 6 in deep:** 8 cubic feet, about 4 bags.
- **4 x 8 ft, 6 in deep:** 16 cubic feet, about 8 bags.
- **4 x 8 ft, 12 in deep:** 32 cubic feet, about 16 bags, roughly 1.2 cubic yards.
- **4 x 8 ft, 18 in deep:** 48 cubic feet, about 24 bags, roughly 1.8 cubic yards.

## How Deep Should It Be?

The depth is decided by the roots, not by the frame you happen to own.

- Six inches suits herbs, lettuce and other shallow crops.
- Ten to twelve inches covers most vegetables and flowers.
- Twelve to eighteen inches suits carrots, parsnips and tomatoes, and helps where the ground below is poor.

If the bed sits on open soil, roots can grow down into it, so you can get away with less. If it sits on concrete or gravel, the bed is the whole root zone and should be filled to the full depth.

## Volume, Weight and Delivery

Bulk soil is sold by the cubic yard; bagged mix by volume, usually 1.5 or 2 cubic feet. A cubic yard of damp topsoil weighs close to a ton, so a pickup load is at its limit long before the bed is full. For anything past about one cubic yard, bulk delivery is cheaper per unit, but you need somewhere to tip it and a route to wheel it.

Bagged mix is easier for one or two beds and lets you choose the blend, but it costs more per cubic foot. Many gardeners mix their own: about 60 per cent topsoil, 30 per cent compost and 10 per cent perlite or coarse sand for drainage.

## Filling Without Regrets

Fill in layers and water each one as you go, so the mix settles before the next layer goes on. Stop about two inches below the rim. That freeboard keeps soil from washing out in heavy rain and gives you room to top up later. Expect the mix to drop by around a tenth of its volume over the first season as air escapes and compost breaks down; keep a bag aside for that top-up.

## Common Mistakes

- Filling with garden soil dug straight from the ground, which compacts and drains badly.
- Skipping the drainage layer on a hard surface.
- Mixing in fresh manure that has not rotted, which burns young roots.
- Filling right to the brim, so the first downpour spills soil over the sides.

## A Quick Sanity Check

Once you know your volume in cubic feet, divide by 27 for cubic yards, or divide by the bag size for the number of bags. For an 8 x 4 bed at a foot deep, that is 32 cubic feet: 32 divided by 27 is 1.19 cubic yards, and 32 divided by 2 is 16 bags. Both routes should agree, which is a good way to catch an arithmetic slip before you order.

## Choosing a Raised Bed Material

The material decides how long the bed lasts and how it looks. Untreated timber is cheap and simple, but it rots within a few years in damp ground. Pressure-treated timber lasts far longer, and modern treatments are considered safe for food crops. Cedar and larch are naturally rot-resistant and need no treatment at all, though they cost more.

Brick, stone and concrete block beds last longest and hold their shape, which matters if the bed is deep or the ground is uneven. They are heavy to build and hard to move, so treat them as permanent. Metal beds, often galvanised steel, are light, long-lasting and warm up quickly in spring, which can help early crops but dries the mix faster in summer.

Whatever you choose, match the bed depth to the crop rather than to the material you happen to have. A shallow frame filled to six inches suits salads and herbs; deeper crops need a taller frame, or a bed sited over ground the roots can grow into.

Line a timber bed with cardboard at the base, and leave the top two inches free, so the mix has room to settle without spilling over the sides in the first heavy rain.

**A typical single-car driveway of 30 x 12 ft at 4 inches compacted needs about 4.4 cubic yards of gravel, which is roughly 6 tons of 3/4-inch crushed stone.** The tonnage varies with the stone, so confirm the figure your supplier uses before ordering.

## Gravel by Driveway Size

These figures use 4 inches compacted and about 1.4 tons per cubic yard.

- **12 x 20 ft:** 80 cubic feet, 3 cubic yards, about 4.2 tons.
- **12 x 30 ft:** 120 cubic feet, 4.4 cubic yards, about 6.2 tons.
- **12 x 40 ft:** 160 cubic feet, 5.9 cubic yards, about 8.3 tons.
- **Double width, 24 x 30 ft:** 240 cubic feet, 8.9 cubic yards, about 12.4 tons.

## Why Depth Drives the Cost

Two inches versus six inches is not a small difference; it is a threefold change in material. For vehicles, four inches compacted is the sensible minimum and six inches is better where the drive takes regular traffic. A loose three-inch layer might look right on the day, but wheels will rut it within a season.

Stone size matters too. Angular crushed stone locks together under a compactor and holds its shape. Rounded pea gravel rolls and ruts, and is better kept for paths and borders than for a drive.

## The Base Nobody Wants to Do

Gravel is only as good as what sits under it. Excavate about four inches, compact the sub-grade, lay a woven landscape fabric, then put the stone down in two layers rather than one. Compact each layer before the next goes on. That is the difference between a drive that lasts years and one that turns into a mud pit at the first wet winter.

## Edging and Drainage

Give the drive an edge. A steel or timber edge set just above the finished level stops the stone spreading into the garden under the wheels. On a slope, add a shallow drainage channel or a french drain along the uphill side, so water does not run down the surface and scour it.

## Bags, Bulk or Tons

Gravel is sold by the bag, the cubic yard or the ton, which makes comparison awkward. Convert everything to the same unit first. A cubic yard of 3/4-inch crushed stone is about 1.4 tons; a 25 kg bag is a small fraction of that, so bags only make sense for a path or a patch. For a full drive, order by the yard or the ton and have it tipped as close to the work as the truck can reach.

## Ordering Checklist

- Measure the finished drive, not the area you are excavating.
- Decide the compacted depth from the traffic, not the budget.
- Add about 10 per cent for settlement and spreading losses.
- Confirm whether the price is per yard or per ton, and whether delivery is included.
- Ask for angular crushed stone, not rounded, for anything driven on.

## Maintaining a Gravel Drive

A gravel drive is not maintenance-free, but the upkeep is small if the base was done well. Once or twice a year, rake the surface to pull stone back from the edges into the middle, where wheels push it aside. If you skip this, the edges thin and the centre ruts.

After a winter of use, top up any hollows with the same grade of stone, then re-compact. Keep a tonne or so aside for this; matching the grade keeps the surface even in colour and texture, and a different stone shows as a patch.

Weed control matters more than it sounds. A few weeds at the edges spread inward, and hand-pulling disturbs the fabric. Treat the edges each spring, and keep the surface swept so debris does not build up and hold moisture against the fabric.

On a sloped drive, check the drainage channel each autumn. Leaves and grit collect there and, if it blocks, water runs down the surface instead of around it, which scours the stone and deepens any ruts. Clearing it takes minutes and prevents the most common cause of drive damage.

**A standard 12 x 10 ft bedroom with 8 ft walls needs about 2 gallons for two coats, after allowing for one door and two windows.** The figure assumes roughly 350 square feet of coverage per gallon, which is typical for a smooth, primed wall.

## Paint by Room Size

These estimates use two coats and subtract one door and two windows.

- **10 x 10 ft:** about 1.5 gallons, so buy 2.
- **12 x 10 ft:** about 1.7 gallons, so buy 2.
- **12 x 12 ft:** about 1.9 gallons, so buy 2.
- **14 x 12 ft:** about 2.2 gallons, so buy 3 for safety.

Ceilings and trim are extra. A ceiling is length x width, and trim is measured in linear feet, usually about a gallon per 100 to 150 feet.

## The Calculation, Step by Step

Add the room's length and width, then double it for the perimeter. Multiply the perimeter by the wall height for the wall area. Subtract about 21 square feet per door and 15 square feet per window. Multiply by the number of coats, then divide by the paint's coverage per gallon.

For a 12 x 10 room with 8 ft walls: the perimeter is 44 ft, wall area is 352 sq ft, minus a door and two windows gives roughly 301 sq ft, two coats is 602 sq ft, and dividing by 350 gives about 1.7 gallons.

## Two Coats, Not One

One coat rarely covers evenly, especially when you are changing colour. Deep colours over pale walls, or pale over deep, often need a primer and sometimes a third coat. Budget for two coats as the default and treat anything less as a bonus.

## Finish and Surface

A smooth, primed surface covers in fewer coats than bare plasterboard or a previously glossed wall. Sand lightly and spot-prime repairs before you start. If the existing finish is glossy, key it or use a bonding primer, or the new paint may not adhere.

## Buying and Storing

Buy all the paint in one go so it comes from a single batch, and keep a labelled tin of each colour for touch-ups. Paint does not match across different batches, and a small tin kept for later is far cheaper than repainting a wall because a mark will not blend.

## Common Mistakes

- Buying for one coat and running short on the second.
- Forgetting to subtract doors and windows, which over-buys by up to a gallon.
- Skipping the primer on a colour change.
- Not accounting for a high ceiling, which adds a surprising amount of wall area.

## A Note on Ceilings and Trim

If you are doing the ceiling, add its area to the wall total before you convert to gallons. Trim, skirting and door frames are painted separately and are easiest to estimate by linear feet. Together these often add 30 to 50 per cent to a bedroom's paint bill, so it is worth pricing them in from the start rather than discovering it at the till.

## Painting Order and Technique

Work from the top down and from the edges inward. Do the ceiling first if it is being painted, then the walls, then the trim and skirting last, so any drips land on surfaces you have not finished yet. Cut in the edges with a brush before rolling, and keep a wet edge so you are never rolling over paint that has started to dry.

Two thin coats beat one thick coat every time. A heavy single coat dries unevenly and hides brush marks poorly, and it is more likely to drip. Let the first coat dry for the time stated on the tin before the second, even if it feels dry to the touch sooner.

Masking tape saves time on trim and around sockets, but press it down firmly and pull it off while the paint is still slightly soft, or it tears the finish. For a neat line, remove the tape at a shallow angle rather than straight up.

Finally, keep the room ventilated while you work and dispose of rags and tins responsibly. Water-based paint cleans up with warm water, but it still needs to cure properly, so avoid washing the walls for a couple of weeks.

faq.a: Around 350 square feet per coat on a smooth, primed surface.

faq.q: Do I need to subtract windows and doors?
faq.a: Yes. Allow about 21 square feet per door and 15 square feet per window.

faq.q: How many coats of paint do I need?
faq.a: Two coats for a colour change, and often two even when refreshing the same colour.

faq.q: Should I buy extra paint?
faq.a: Keep about 10% spare for touch-ups, and note the colour code for future matching.

body_markdown:
**A 10 x 10 ft room has 100 square feet of floor. With 12 x 12 inch tiles that is 100 tiles, or about 110 once you add the 10 per cent waste allowance.** Change the tile size and the count changes, even though the floor does not.

## Tiles by Size for a 100 Square Foot Floor

- **12 x 12 in (1 sq ft each):** 100 tiles, buy about 110.
- **12 x 24 in (2 sq ft each):** 50 tiles, buy about 55.
- **6 x 6 in (0.25 sq ft each):** 400 tiles, buy about 440.
- **8 x 8 in (0.44 sq ft each):** 225 tiles, buy about 248.

## Tiles, Boxes and Coverage

Tile is usually sold by the box, and the box states its coverage in square feet rather than a tile count. Read that figure first. A box covering 10 square feet means you need about 11 boxes for a 100 square foot floor with waste, whatever the tile count happens to be. Buying by box coverage avoids the arithmetic entirely.

## Why Add 10 Per Cent

Cuts, breakages and pattern matching all consume tile. A straight grid loses about 10 per cent to edge cuts and the odd broken tile. A diagonal or diamond layout turns every edge into a triangle cut and pushes the waste toward 15 per cent. Herringbone wastes more again. Buying all the tile at once also keeps it from a single dye lot, so the floor is one colour rather than a patchwork.

## Plan the Layout From the Centre

Mark the centre of the room and work outward so the cut tiles at opposite walls are the same width. That looks deliberate. Starting from one corner leaves a full tile on one side and a sliver on the other, which is the first thing anyone notices. In a doorway, dry-lay a row so the two rooms meet on a full tile if you can.

## Grout Lines

Grout joints add a small amount back. If you are working to an exact grid, allow a couple of millimetres per tile, which can shift the count on a large floor. For most rooms the waste allowance already covers this, but check if you are laying large-format tiles with wide joints.

## Common Mistakes

- Ordering the exact area and ignoring cuts.
- Mixing dye lots from different orders.
- Counting tiles instead of checking the box coverage.
- Returning every spare box, then having nothing left for a future repair.

## Keep a Spare Box

Keep one unopened box aside. Flooring takes damage over the years, and a matching tile from the same batch is the only way to repair it invisibly. A spare box is a small cost now and a large saving later.

## Tools and Preparation for Laying Tile

On a floor this size, a few tools make the difference between a neat job and a frustrating one. You need a notched trowel, a tile cutter, spacers, a spirit level, a rubber mallet, and a bucket for mixing adhesive. For large-format tiles, add a levelling clip system to stop the corners from lipping where two tiles meet.

The floor must be flat, clean and dry before you start. Check the flatness with a straight edge laid in several directions; a small hump or hollow will show through the finished floor. If the floor is uneven, level it first, because no amount of care in laying will hide it afterwards.

Plan the layout before the first tile goes down. Mark the centre lines, dry-lay a row in each direction, and check the cuts at every wall. On a 10 x 10 room, working from the centre usually gives you even cut tiles on opposite walls, which looks deliberate rather than accidental.

Work in small sections so the adhesive does not skin over before you place the tile, and check the level as you go rather than at the very end.

faq.q: How much extra tile should I buy?
faq.a: Add 10% for straight layouts and 15% for diagonal or patterned work.

faq.q: How many tiles in a box?
faq.a: It varies by size; check the box coverage in square feet rather than counting tiles.

faq.q: Do I need to account for grout lines?
faq.a: Yes for precise work, though the waste allowance usually covers the small difference.

faq.q: Can I return leftover tile?
faq.a: Often yes if unopened and from the same batch, but dye lots differ, so buy all you need at once.

body_markdown:
**Overseeding uses about 2 pounds of grass seed per 1,000 square feet, which is 0.002 pounds per square foot.** That is half the rate of a brand-new lawn, because you are thickening an existing sward rather than starting from bare soil.

## Overseeding Rate by Area

At the overseeding rate of about 2 lb per 1,000 sq ft:

- **500 sq ft:** about 1 lb.
- **1,000 sq ft:** about 2 lb.
- **2,500 sq ft:** about 5 lb.
- **5,000 sq ft:** about 10 lb.

For comparison, a new lawn wants roughly 4 to 5 lb per 1,000 sq ft, which is more than double. Using the new-lawn rate when overseeding wastes seed and can smother the thin grass you are trying to help.

## Why the Rate Is Lower

When you overseed, existing plants already cover much of the ground. You are filling gaps, not establishing a lawn from nothing. Too much seed and the seedlings compete with each other and with the established grass, and the weakest of them die. The right rate gives you density without waste.

## Prepare the Ground First

Seed fails more often from poor preparation than from the wrong rate. Mow the lawn short, scarify or rake out thatch and dead material, and aerate if the ground is compacted. Seed needs contact with soil. If it sits on top of thatch it will dry out and never germinate. After sowing, a thin top-dressing of compost helps, but keep the seed near the surface.

## Timing

Early autumn is the easiest window. The soil is still warm, rain is more reliable, and weeds are slowing down. Spring works too, but the young grass then has to survive summer heat while it is still shallow-rooted. Avoid sowing in the heat of midsummer unless you can water reliably.

## Watering and Aftercare

Keep the top inch of soil damp for the first two weeks, using light, frequent watering rather than one heavy soak. Once the new grass is up and has been cut twice, switch to deeper, less frequent watering so the roots go down. Stay off the lawn until the new plants are rooted, or you will pull them out as you walk.

## Common Mistakes

- Using the new-lawn rate and wasting half the seed.
- Sowing onto thatch or hard ground without preparation.
- Letting the seed dry out in the first fortnight.
- Sowing too deep, where the seed cannot reach the light.

## A Simple Rule

If you remember nothing else, remember this: overseeding is about half the rate of a new lawn. Work out your area in square feet, divide by 1,000, and multiply by two. Round up to the next bag, and keep a little spare for the thin patches you will spot a month later.

## Choosing a Seed Mix for Overseeding

The best mix for overseeding is one that matches or complements what is already growing. If the existing lawn is mostly ryegrass and fescue, using a similar mix means the new grass grows at the same rate and knits into the old. Introducing a very different grass can leave visible patches of different colour and texture.

For a shaded lawn, look for a mix high in fescue, which tolerates lower light under trees and beside walls. For a lawn that takes heavy use, choose a mix leaning on ryegrass for wear tolerance. Read the label for the proportions rather than the picture on the front.

Buy fresh seed and check the sow-by date. Seed germinates less well as it ages, and old seed produces an uneven result that is hard to distinguish from poor preparation. Store any spare in a cool, dry place, sealed against damp and mice.

Note down the mix you used. When you top up thin patches in future, matching the mix keeps the lawn one colour, and it makes the job far easier than guessing at what was sown before.

faq.a: About 4 to 5 pounds for a new lawn, and 2 pounds when overseeding an existing one.

faq.q: What is the best time to sow grass seed?
faq.a: Early autumn, when the soil is warm and weeds are slowing down.

faq.q: How long until grass seed grows?
faq.a: Seven to fourteen days for ryegrass, up to three weeks for bluegrass.

faq.q: Should I cover grass seed with soil?
faq.a: A thin layer of compost or topsoil helps, but leave the seed near the surface so it can sprout.

body_markdown:
**A 10 x 10 ft slab at 4 inches thick needs about 1.23 cubic yards of concrete, which is roughly 56 bags of 80 lb mix or 74 bags of 60 lb mix.** The thickness you choose changes the count a lot, so decide that before you buy.

## Bags by Slab Thickness

These use an 80 lb bag yielding about 0.6 cubic feet.

- **10 x 10 ft at 4 in:** 33.3 cubic feet, about 56 bags.
- **10 x 10 ft at 5 in:** 41.7 cubic feet, about 70 bags.
- **10 x 10 ft at 6 in:** 50 cubic feet, about 84 bags.

With 60 lb bags, yielding about 0.45 cubic feet, add roughly a third more: about 74 bags at 4 inches.

## Is Bagged Mix the Right Choice?

Probably not at this size. Past about one cubic yard, ready-mix concrete delivered by truck is faster, cheaper per unit and far less work. The catch is that a pour cannot wait: you need the base prepared, the formwork set and helpers on hand before the truck arrives. Most suppliers also have a minimum load, so very small jobs price badly either way.

Bagged mix suits small pours: fence post footings, a garden step, a small pad or a repair. A 10 x 10 slab is near the upper limit of what is sensible to mix by hand, and doing it in one continuous pour with bags is hard work.

## Getting the Volume Right

Multiply length by width to get the area, multiply by the thickness in feet, and divide by 27 for cubic yards. For a 10 x 10 slab at 4 inches: 100 x 0.333 is 33.3 cubic feet, and dividing by 27 gives 1.23 cubic yards. Divide by the bag yield for the bag count.

## Prepare the Base

A slab is only as good as its base. Compact the ground, add a gravel sub-base for drainage, and set formwork so the slab is a true rectangle. For a slab that carries vehicles, lay reinforcement mesh in the lower third before the pour. Skipping this is the usual reason a slab cracks in its first winter.

## Mixing and Curing

Mix only what you can place within about half an hour, and mix it stiff rather than wet. Extra water makes concrete easier to move but weaker when it sets; use the amount stated on the bag. After the pour, keep the slab covered and let it cure slowly for several days rather than drying it in the sun, and cut control joints so any cracking happens in a straight line where you want it.

## Ordering Checklist

- Fix the thickness from what the slab carries, before counting bags.
- Add about 5 to 10 per cent for spillage and uneven ground.
- Compare the bag cost against ready-mix per cubic yard, including the minimum charge.
- Have formwork, mesh and helpers ready before either route.

## Tools and Safety for a Slab Pour

A slab this size needs proper preparation and a team. Have mixing tubs or a hired mixer, shovels, a rake, a float and trowel, a screed board, and formwork boards with pegs. For 56 bags of mix you will want at least two or three people, because once the pour begins it cannot stop.

Work out where the water and the mixed concrete will come from and go before you start. Concrete is heavy, and carting it across a garden slows everything down. If a truck can reach the site, ready-mix removes most of this work, but the area must be prepared and the helpers ready when it arrives.

Wear gloves and eye protection, and avoid kneeling in the wet mix, which dries and burns the skin. Mix in a ventilated spot, and mix only what you can place within about half an hour.

Set the formwork square and peg it firmly before mixing anything, and lay any reinforcement on spacers so it sits within the slab rather than on the ground. Clean tools straight after the pour; set concrete is far harder to remove than wet.

faq.q: How many bags of concrete make a cubic yard?
faq.a: About 45 bags of 80 lb mix, or 60 bags of 60 lb mix, per cubic yard.

faq.q: How thick should a concrete slab be?
faq.a: Four inches for paths and patios, five to six inches for driveways and heavy loads.

faq.q: How much water do I add to concrete mix?
faq.a: Follow the bag instructions; roughly 3 quarts per 80 lb bag, added gradually.

faq.q: Can I pour concrete over soil?
faq.a: Yes if the ground is compacted and level, with a gravel base for drainage.
